content: A Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) is a specialized area within a hospital dedicated to the care of critically ill infants, children, and teenagers. The PICU is typically overseen by one or more pediatric intensivists or PICU consultants, and it is staffed by doctors and nurses who have undergone specialized training and possess extensive experience in pediatric intensive care. In addition to these core staff members, the unit may also include nurse practitioners, respiratory therapists, physician assistants, physiotherapists, social workers, and clerks, although the composition of the team can vary significantly depending on the geographic location of the hospital. The ratio of healthcare professionals to patients in the PICU is generally higher than in other hospital departments, reflecting the severity of the patients' conditions and the potential for life-threatening complications. The PICU frequently utilizes advanced medical technology and equipment, such as mechanical ventilators and sophisticated patient monitoring systems, to provide the highest level of care. Due to the complexity of care and the resources required, PICUs typically operate with a larger budget compared to many other hospital departments. The first pediatric intensive care unit, referred to as a pediatric emergency ward, was established in 1955 by Goran Haglund. By the early 1960s, infants were being intubated for extended periods, marking a significant advancement in critical care. The introduction of breathing tubes made from polyvinyl chloride (PVC) allowed clinicians to avoid performing tracheostomies in many children who required prolonged mechanical ventilation, thereby reducing the need for this invasive surgical procedure.
